direct_answer:
Repsol states that it conducted a CSRD-aligned double materiality assessment based on EFRAG ESRS standards and EFRAG implementation guidance, covering the entire value chain and to be reviewed annually [Source 7]. It followed five phases: (1) analysis of context and business model, (2) stakeholder mapping and consultation, (3) identification of topics and potentially material impacts/risks/opportunities (IROs), (4) evaluation of IROs, and (5) results and validation [Source 7].

Stakeholder input was incorporated via consultation of 7 stakeholder groups (employees, suppliers, shareholders and investors, NGOs, public administrations, contractors, customers and society), generating more than 550 responses through online questionnaires, interviews and working groups; five other stakeholder groups were not consulted directly and were instead assessed using public information, analysis and internal consultations with the company areas managing those stakeholders [Source 8]. Repsol also indicates that human rights due diligence processes (to identify, prevent, mitigate and remedy risks and social impacts) were taken into account in the materiality assessment during identification and evaluation of IROs [Source 8].

For impact materiality, expert areas scored (1–5) the extent of effect, irremediability and probability, while stakeholders scored magnitude (severity/benefit) at topic/sub-topic level (1–5); impact materiality was calculated as the average of severity variables (scope, irremediability, magnitude) multiplied by probability, with a more conservative approach for environmental impacts where high irremediability can predominate [Source 15]. For financial materiality (risks/opportunities), expert areas assessed the potential magnitude of annual financial effects across three time horizons (generally based on operating result before taxes) and probability (based on historical statistics or expert judgement); the product was mapped to a 1–5 scale built with the company’s annual operating result [Source 15]. Repsol links this to its ISO 31000 / COSO ERM-aligned integrated risk management; the risk-map area also participates in the double materiality assessment to ensure consistency and integration, and lower-severity risks not in the risk map receive a specific qualitative/quantitative assessment per the financial materiality methodology [Source 1].

Results were validated/evaluated by the Sustainability Division, the risk team and business managers, presented to a CSRD-focused steering committee on sustainability information (with management participation from representative businesses/corporate areas), and presented to the Board Sustainability Committee under internal control arrangements [Source 3]. Repsol reports identifying 44 material impacts and 17 material risks and opportunities, and that topic/sub-topic materiality is determined by the highest-valued IRO within each topic/sub-topic; the threshold for determining impact and financial materiality is the average value of the valuations [Source 1].

Sustainability matters identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective are not explicitly listed in the retrieved passages. The passages do indicate that climate change/energy transition-related risks are material and can affect performance (financial perspective) [Source 12], and that Repsol identified material impacts, risks and opportunities across environmental, social and governance aspects [Source 12]. However, the retrieved evidence does not provide a definitive list of sustainability matters that are simultaneously material on both dimensions. The only explicit statement on dual-dimension outcome in the retrieved passages is that biodiversity and ecosystems is material from an impact perspective but not from a financial perspective [Source 10].
compliance_rationale: The retrieved passages provide substantial evidence on the double materiality assessment process (phases, stakeholder consultation approach, scoring/threshold methodology for impact and financial materiality, linkage to risk management, and governance/validation) [Sources 1, 3, 7, 8, 15]. However, they do not provide the required outcome detail for the question—i.e., a clear list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives—so full ESRS 1 outcome transparency cannot be evidenced from the provided excerpts [Sources 10, 12].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives (double-material) is not provided in the retrieved passages.
Clear mapping of each material topic/sub-topic to whether it is impact material, financial material, or both (e.g., a double materiality matrix/table) is not included in the retrieved passages.
Details on the five stakeholder groups not directly consulted (which groups, and how their views were inferred) are not specified in the retrieved passages.

Value-chain boundary specifics (which upstream/downstream segments were assessed for each topic) are not fully detailed in the retrieved passages; some topic-specific sections note parts of own operations out of scope and lack of consultations with potentially affected communities [Sources 4, 10].
key_findings: Double materiality assessment is based on EFRAG ESRS and EFRAG implementation guidance, covers the entire value chain, and is reviewed annually [Source 7].
Methodology comprises five phases: context/business model; stakeholder map & consultation; identification of topics and potentially material IROs; evaluation; results & validation [Source 7].
Stakeholder consultation covered 7 groups with >550 responses; 5 groups were not directly consulted and were assessed via public information and internal consultations [Source 8].

Impact materiality scoring uses extent/scope, irremediability, probability (experts) and magnitude (stakeholders); impact materiality computed as average severity × probability, with conservative treatment for environmental impacts where high irremediability can dominate [Source 15].

Financial materiality scoring uses magnitude of annual financial effects (generally based on operating result before taxes) and probability; mapped to a 1–5 scale based on annual operating result [Source 15].

Process is integrated with ISO 31000 / COSO ERM risk management; risk-map participants also participate in double materiality; lower-severity risks outside the risk map get additional qualitative/quantitative assessment [Source 1].

Repsol reports 44 material impacts and 17 material risks/opportunities; thresholds for impact and financial materiality are based on average valuation; topic/sub-topic materiality uses the highest-valued IRO within the topic/sub-topic [Source 1].
Biodiversity and ecosystems is explicitly concluded to be impact-material but not financially material [Source 10].
